title: Vertibird Weather
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 12 of 40
content:
Vertibirds had weather.

No one warned me about that.

On the ground, weather was rain, wind, heat, radstorms, and the occasional piece of metal traveling fast enough to count as a local climate. In a vertibird, weather was all of those things plus gravity developing opinions.

Danse loved flying.

He would deny this if asked directly, so I did not ask directly.

I watched instead.

The moment we cleared the Prydwen’s flight deck, something in his shoulders relaxed. He sat near the open side with one hand on the overhead grip, scanning the city below. The wind pulled at his hair. His expression was alert but peaceful.

“You like this,” I said.

He looked over.

“Operational mobility is useful.”

“That was not a denial.”

“I don’t know what you want from me.”

“Joy.”

“That seems excessive.”

The vertibird hit turbulence.

My stomach attempted desertion.

Danse caught the front of my harness before I could slide half a foot across the bench.

“Secure yourself.”

“I am secured.”

“Poorly.”

“Blame whoever designed a seatbelt for people wearing combat armor.”

He leaned closer and tightened the strap himself.

His knuckles brushed my ribs through my coat.

I forgot the turbulence.

Danse noticed my sudden stillness.

His hands paused.

We were close enough that I could see a tiny nick in his lower lip, probably from shaving too quickly.

“Too tight?” he asked.

“No.”

His eyes remained on mine a fraction too long.

Then he sat back.

“Good.”

The mission was simple by Brotherhood standards: survey a collapsed research building, recover data, kill anything hostile enough to object.

By Commonwealth standards, that meant three hours underground, two packs of ferals, one automated turret, and a ceiling collapse that trapped us in a laboratory with a door fused shut.

Danse examined it.

“Thermal damage.”

“Can you open it?”

“Yes.”

He tried.

The door did not move.

I leaned against the wall.

“Outstanding.”

He gave me a look.

“We need leverage.”

We found a length of pipe. Together we wedged it into the seam.

“On three,” he said.

“You mean one, two, three, push? Or one, two, push on three?”

Danse closed his eyes.

“Why would anyone push before three?”

“You would be amazed.”

“On three.”

We pushed.

The pipe bent.

The door remained.

Danse swore.

I laughed.

“This amuses you?”

“A little.”

“We’re trapped.”

“With supplies, weapons, and a radio.”

“The signal won’t penetrate this depth.”

“Still funny that you swore.”

He stared at me.

“You’ve heard me swear.”

“Not at a door.”

“That’s your standard?”

“I contain multitudes.”

He sat on an overturned cabinet.

For twenty minutes we tried every practical solution.

Then we stopped.

The room became quiet.

An emergency light pulsed over us, red then dark, red then dark.

Danse removed his gloves and flexed his hands.

“Blisters?” I asked.

“No.”

“Let me see.”

“I’m fine.”

“Danse.”

He held out one hand.

There was a shallow cut across his palm from the bent pipe.

I pulled a small antiseptic packet from my bag.

“It’s nothing.”

“So was my coat at ArcJet, according to you.”

“That was different.”

“How?”

He had no answer.

I cleaned the cut.

His hand was rough from weapons, tools, and years of work. He watched my fingers move over his palm with an intensity that made the room feel warmer.

“You know,” I said, because silence was becoming dangerous, “for someone covered in advanced military technology most of the time, you get injured in extremely mundane ways.”

“Occupational hazard.”

“Pipe doors.”

“Very dangerous.”

“Coffee.”

“I have never been injured by coffee.”

“Your taste has.”

He laughed.

Actually laughed.

A low, surprised sound that seemed to escape before he could stop it.

I looked up.

Danse looked almost offended.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“I do that sometimes.”

His hand remained in mine.

Neither of us mentioned it.

Eventually we found another route: a maintenance crawlspace above the laboratory.

Danse hated it.

Power armor had to stay behind while we squeezed through the narrow shaft. Without it, he moved more quietly but seemed oddly exposed.

Halfway through, the metal beneath me groaned.

“Stop,” he said.

I froze.

He was behind me.

“Move your weight to the crossbeam.”

“Which one?”

His hand settled at my hip to guide me.

Every thought I had vanished.

“There,” he said.

His voice was close to my ear.

I shifted carefully.

The panel held.

Danse removed his hand at once.

“Continue.”

Neither of us spoke until we reached the other side.

We returned to the Prydwen after dark with the data secured and the damaged power armor retrieved.

As the vertibird climbed, Danse sat beside me instead of across from me.

Our shoulders touched whenever the aircraft banked.

This time neither of us moved away.

Below us, the Commonwealth looked almost beautiful.

Danse watched the horizon.

I watched him.

When he caught me, I expected a question.

Instead he looked back at the city and said, “The view is better from this side.”

I knew he was giving me an excuse.

I took it.

“Yes,” I said. “It is.”

On the return flight from our first supply run, the weather turned mean.

The pilot warned us about turbulence. Danse answered with the calm acknowledgement of a man who considered gravity a subordinate officer.

I tightened my harness.

“You can admit you hate this too.”

“I don’t hate vertibirds.”

The aircraft dropped hard enough to lift my stomach into my throat.

Danse’s hand clamped around the overhead strap.

“Your knuckles disagree.”

“My knuckles are maintaining stability.”

“Heroically.”

The pilot laughed over the intercom.

Danse glared toward the cockpit.

Another gust shoved us sideways.

A crate broke loose from its floor clamp.

Danse was out of his seat before I registered it. He caught the crate with one boot, shoved it back, and locked the damaged clamp with a spare length of webbing.

“Stay seated,” he ordered.

“You are also not seated.”

“I’m securing equipment.”

“I was going to help.”

“And now you are going to remain secured.”

I crossed my arms.

He returned to his seat, buckled in, and looked at me.

“What?”

“That was very romantic.”

His expression went blank.

“The crate?”

“No. Ordering me into a chair.”

“I was preventing injury.”

“Exactly. Swoon.”

He stared for three seconds.

Then his mouth betrayed him.

The smile was small, but real.

“You have a strange definition of romance.”

“You gave me a laser rifle and called it recognition of service.”

“That was not romantic.”

“Your track record is against you.”

The aircraft dipped again.

This time my stomach lost the argument entirely.

I went quiet.

Danse noticed at once.

“You all right?”

“Fine.”

He gave me the look I usually gave him.

“That is not a useful answer.”

“I’m reconsidering my relationship with the sky.”

His expression softened.

“Look at me.”

I did.

“Not outside. The horizon movement makes it worse.”

“You have experience with this?”

“First deployment. I was sick through half the flight.”

I blinked.

“Paladin Danse gets airsick?”

“Got.”

“Oh, this is precious information.”

“If you repeat it, I will deny everything.”

“Noted.”

Another rough pocket shook the cabin.

Danse kept talking.

Not about the flight. About maintenance schedules. About how Brotherhood pilots learned to read crosswinds around ruined skyscrapers. About a mechanic at the Citadel who once painted a deathclaw on a vertibird’s nose and got three days of disciplinary duty for it.

The stories were not particularly important.

That was the point.

Danse kept talking because he had noticed silence made the vertibird worse for me.

He told me about a lancer who once tried to land during a dust storm and came down on a pre-War billboard. He described the resulting lecture from Kells with such precise mimicry that I stared at him.

“You do impressions?”

“No.”

“That was absolutely an impression.”

“It was an accurate reconstruction.”

“Of his voice.”

“Relevant to the story.”

The aircraft dropped hard enough to make my stomach climb into my throat. My hand tightened over his.

Danse did not comment.

Instead he continued. “The billboard said ‘See Scenic Boston.’”

I laughed despite the turbulence.

“That’s cruel.”

“The lancer was unharmed.”

“So you’re allowed to laugh?”

“I did not say I laughed.”

“You remember the sign.”

“That proves nothing.”

Another shudder. His thumb pressed once against the side of my hand.

“Look at me,” he said.

I did.

“Not outside. The horizon makes it worse when we bank.”

“How do you know?”

“I’ve transported enough recruits.”

“And how many held your hand?”

His ears reddened.

“None.”

“Excellent. I enjoy exclusive training benefits.”

Danse looked toward the open door with tremendous interest.

But he did not pull away.

His voice gave me something steady to hold onto.

By the time the Prydwen came into view, my stomach had mostly returned to its assigned location.

“Better?” he asked.

“Yes.”

He nodded.

I looked at our hands.

At some point during the worst of the turbulence, his had ended up palm-down on the bench between us.

Mine rested over it.

Neither of us seemed able to identify when that happened.

Danse looked too.

His thumb moved once beneath my fingers.

“Atmospheric conditions,” I said.

“Obviously.”

“Safety procedure.”

“Clearly.”

Neither of us moved our hands until the landing gear touched the deck.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
